articles.title: The Steel Bars on the Roof
articles.dek: All over the Philippines, houses stand with rusting steel reaching into empty sky. Abraham lived the same way for a hundred years, and Hebrews says God was proud to be called his God.
articles.quote: Faith leaves the steel bars standing, because the One who drew the plans has promised to finish the house.
articles.illustration: Filipino houses with rebar left standing
articles.body:
Drive through almost any town in the Philippines and you will see them: concrete houses with steel bars sticking out of the roof slab, rusting gently as they reach into empty air. Visitors from abroad sometimes assume the builders ran out of money or simply forgot to finish. Filipinos read those bars differently. The bakal left standing at the top of each column is a promise made of steel, and it means a second floor is coming someday, when there is enough.

Picture one such house in a barangay outside Lipa. Mang Ernesto and his wife Nita poured the first floor in 1998, using money saved from his tricycle route and her small carinderia. When the mason asked whether he should cut the column bars flush with the slab, Ernesto shook his head and said, "Iwan mo." Leave them. For twenty years those bars stood through typhoon after typhoon, and the neighbors hung laundry from them while the children tied strings to them for kites. Once a cousin laughed and said the house looked like it was waiting for something, and Nita answered, "It is."

The second floor finally went up when their eldest, by then a nurse, sent home enough for hollow blocks and cement. Ernesto stood in the yard as the masons tied new steel onto the old bars, and he cried a little, because those bars had waited so long. Yet he told his children something surprising afterward. In all those years, the house had never felt unfinished to him, because every time he looked up at the roof he could already see the room where they would sleep.

That is very close to the way the Letter to the Hebrews describes faith. Hebrews was written to Jewish believers in Jesus who had already paid a real price for following him. The writer reminds them of the days when they "endured in a great conflict full of suffering," when they were publicly insulted and "joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property" (Heb 10:32–34). Now, years later, they were tired. The promises of God felt slow, and some were tempted to drift back to an easier life. So the writer says, "We do not belong to those who shrink back and are destroyed, but to those who have faith and are saved" (Heb 10:39), and then opens a gallery of men and women who kept going when the finished house was nowhere in sight.

The gallery begins with a definition: "Now faith is confidence in what we hope for and assurance about what we do not see" (Heb 11:1). The Greek word behind "confidence" is hypostasis, which literally describes something that stands underneath, a foundation. In the everyday Greek of the period, the word could also turn up in property records, where it carried the sense of a title deed. One way to read the verse, then, is that faith is like holding the papers to a house you have not yet walked into. The house is real, and you have the document in your hand, though you are still standing in the yard.

No one in Scripture lived that way longer than Abraham. He was seventy-five years old, settled and prosperous in the city of Haran, when God told him, "Go from your country, your people and your father's household to the land I will show you" (Gen 12:1). Imagine the scene: the camels loaded, the servants asking which road to take, and Abraham unable to answer. Hebrews puts it plainly: he "obeyed and went, even though he did not know where he was going" (Heb 11:8).

What happened when he arrived is the part most of us forget. He never built a house there. "By faith he made his home in the promised land like a stranger in a foreign country; he lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise" (Heb 11:9). For about a hundred years, across three generations, the family that God promised the whole land of Canaan lived in goat-hair tents. The only piece of ground Abraham ever owned there was a burial cave. When Sarah died, he went to the Hittites and said, "I am a foreigner and stranger among you. Sell me some property for a burial site here so I can bury my dead" (Gen 23:4), and he paid four hundred shekels of silver for it (Gen 23:16). His one title deed in the promised land was a grave.

Hebrews explains how a man could live like that without bitterness:

"For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God." (Heb 11:10)

The two words the writer uses for God are worth a closer look. Technitēs, translated "architect," is the designer, the one who draws the plan. Dēmiourgos, translated "builder," is the one who actually lays the stones and gets the work done. The writer deliberately puts both in God's hands. Abraham could live in a tent with his head held high because the city was already on God's drawing board, and the One who drew it had also promised to build it. Seen this way, Abraham's grave in Canaan becomes something like Ernesto's steel bars. He planted himself in the land he did not yet possess, as if to say, "This is where my family's story continues."

The writer then says something tender about all these pilgrims: "All these people were still living by faith when they died. They did not receive the things promised; they only saw them and welcomed them from a distance" (Heb 11:13). The verb for "welcomed," aspazomai, is the ordinary word for greeting someone. Every Filipino family knows the scene at the airport arrival area, where relatives press against the barrier and wave wildly at a loved one still far down the corridor. The traveler is not yet in their arms, but the joy has already started. That is how Abraham greeted the promises of God, with a full heart, years before they arrived.

Then comes the line that must have lifted those weary first readers to their feet. Because these people longed "for a better country, a heavenly one," the writer says, "God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them" (Heb 11:16). God was proud to put his name beside people who lived in tents, people whose lives looked unfinished to every neighbor who passed by.

Most of us have some rebar on the roof. It may be a degree you had to pause, a marriage that is being slowly rebuilt, a son or daughter who has wandered far from God, or savings that keep disappearing into hospital bills and school fees. It is easy to feel embarrassed by those unfinished places and tempting to cut the bars flush so no one can see what is missing. Hebrews invites you to leave them standing. Faith leaves the steel bars standing, because the One who drew the plans has promised to finish the house.

Before the day ends, you might name one unfinished part of your life and bring it to God as a promise held in trust, perhaps by writing it on a small card and keeping it in your Bible with Hebrews 11:10 written beneath it. When you look at it in the weeks ahead, you can greet that promise from a distance the way Abraham did, with gratitude instead of shame. Some of what God is building you will see in this life, as Ernesto saw his second floor. The rest is waiting in a city with foundations, designed and built by a God who is glad, even now, to be called yours.

articles.title: When Words Stop Working
articles.dek: God told Ezekiel to pack a bag and dig through a wall while his neighbors watched. Behind that strange command is one small Hebrew word that reveals how far love will go to be understood.
articles.quote: When the people we love can no longer hear our words, love does not fall silent; it finds a way to be seen.
articles.body:
Florence Nightingale came home from the Crimean War in 1856 carrying a number she could not forget. In the military hospital at Scutari, far more British soldiers had died of disease, of filth and fever and bad drains, than had ever died of wounds from the battlefield. She had seen the men die. Now she had to convince the generals and politicians in London, who preferred reports that said everything was under control. She knew from experience that they would not read long columns of figures. In a letter she described her plan: she would try "to affect thro' the Eyes what we fail to convey to the public through their word-proof ears."

Working with the statistician William Farr, she drew what became known as her rose diagrams, circles cut into wedges like slices of a cake, one for each month of the war. The wedges were colored by cause of death, and the blue wedges for preventable disease swallowed everything else on the page. A busy official could understand them in ten seconds. Her charts helped push the army toward sanitary reform, and the lessons spread into hospitals around the world. Nightingale had already spoken plenty of words. When those words bounced off, she loved those soldiers enough to find another way to make people see.

Twenty-four centuries earlier, God did something very similar with a priest named Ezekiel.

Ezekiel lived among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. In 597 BC the Babylonians had taken King Jehoiachin and thousands of Jerusalem's leading citizens into captivity, and Ezekiel was among them. Back home, Jerusalem still stood, with a puppet king named Zedekiah on the throne. The exiles clung to the hope that it would stay standing and that they would soon be going home. Chapter 11 ends with Ezekiel coming out of a vision and doing what a prophet does: "I told the exiles everything the LORD had shown me" (Ezekiel 11:25). The vision had shown God's glory leaving the temple and the city. It was the hardest news a Jew could hear, and the people sitting in front of Ezekiel did not want to hear it.

So God changed the method. He diagnosed the problem first: "Son of man, you are living among a rebellious people. They have eyes to see but do not see and ears to hear but do not hear" (Ezekiel 12:2). Then he gave Ezekiel something to do.

"Therefore, son of man, pack your belongings for exile and in the daytime, as they watch, set out and go from where you are to another place. Perhaps they will understand, though they are a rebellious people." (Ezekiel 12:3)

Imagine it. In broad daylight, a respected priest carried his sleeping mat, his water jar and his few clothes out of his house and stacked them by the door, the way refugees pack. At evening, with the neighbors gathering, he knelt and dug through the mud-brick wall of his own house with his bare hands. Then he hoisted the bundle onto his shoulder, covered his face, and walked out into the dusk. "So I did as I was commanded," he writes simply, "carrying them on my shoulders while they watched" (Ezekiel 12:7).

It worked, at least in one sense. The next morning God said, "Son of man, did not the Israelites, that rebellious people, ask you, 'What are you doing?'" (Ezekiel 12:9). Sermons had not made them curious, but a man digging through his own wall did. Ezekiel's answer was short: "I am a sign to you" (Ezekiel 12:11). The Hebrew word for sign here is mofet, a word used elsewhere for the wonders of the Exodus. It means a portent, a living exhibit, something that points beyond itself. Ezekiel was explaining that the people still in Jerusalem would soon flee in exactly this way, and that their prince would slip out through a gap in the wall at night with his face covered (Ezekiel 12:12). The detail is haunting, because that is what happened. When Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, Zedekiah fled by night through a gate between the walls, was captured, and was blinded before he was taken to Babylon (2 Kings 25:4–7). God had said he would be brought to Babylon "but he will not see it" (Ezekiel 12:13).

The most tender word in the whole passage is easy to pass over. It is the Hebrew word 'ulay, translated "perhaps" in verse 3: "Perhaps they will understand." This is God speaking. He has just called these people rebellious three times in two verses, and he knows them better than they know themselves. He still uses the word that hopeful parents and patient friends use. Perhaps this time. Perhaps this way. The whole sign was an act of hope aimed at people who had given God little reason to hope. One way to read this chapter, then, is as a picture of the heart of God toward a family member who has stopped listening. He does not give up on them, and he does not simply repeat himself louder. He looks for a new door into their understanding, even if it means asking his servant to dig one through a wall.

The cost fell on Ezekiel. He was already an exile; he did not need to rehearse losing his home. Yet he gave up his dignity, his evening and part of his house so that his neighbors might finally understand. The New Testament carries this same pattern to its fullest. On the night before the cross, Jesus did not lecture his disciples about humility. He took a towel and washed their feet, and then said, "I have set you an example that you should do as I have done for you" (John 13:15). The apostle John later put it plainly: "Dear children, let us not love with words or speech but with actions and in truth" (1 John 3:18).

Most of us know a person with word-proof ears. It may be a teenager who rolls their eyes before you finish a sentence, or a father who has heard every speech about his drinking. It may be a sibling who has long since stopped answering your messages about God, or a coworker who has learned to tune out anything that sounds like a sermon. We are tempted to say it again, louder and with more Bible verses attached. Ezekiel 12 suggests a different kind of persistence, where love keeps the hope of that little word 'ulay and looks for a way to make the truth visible.

For you, that sign may be very ordinary. It might mean showing up at your brother's house with lunch and leaving without bringing up the old argument. It could mean apologizing first to your teenager, out loud, in front of the family, so that they can watch what repentance looks like. It might be the way you handle a loss at work, calmly and without bitterness, while someone who does not believe is quietly watching. These acts can feel small and even a little foolish, much as Ezekiel must have felt with dirt under his fingernails. But people who will not read a sermon will often watch a life, and sooner or later many of them ask the same question the exiles asked: "What are you doing?"

Ezekiel 12 also has a word for the one who is tired of waiting. The chapter closes with God answering people who said every vision comes to nothing: "None of my words will be delayed any longer; whatever I say will be fulfilled" (Ezekiel 12:28). The God who kept his word to Jerusalem will keep his promises to you, including his promise to work in the people you love.

So think of one person whose ears have closed to your words, and ask God today for one quiet action that could speak in their place. When the people we love can no longer hear our words, love does not fall silent; it finds a way to be seen. Carry that small Hebrew word with you as you go: perhaps. God still says it about the people we pray for, and on our hardest days, he still says it about us.

articles.title: Honey on the Alphabet
articles.dek: Nine hundred years ago, Jewish children licked honey off their first Bible lesson. Psalm 119 suggests God still teaches his children to taste his words that way.
articles.quote: Everyone meditates on something all day long; the psalmist taught his restless mind to come home to the words of God.
articles.body:
Before sunrise on the spring feast of Shavuot, somewhere in the towns of northern France or the Rhineland around the year 1100, a small boy of about five was wrapped in a cloak and carried through the dark streets to his teacher's house. He was carried so that nothing unclean along the road would touch him on this particular morning. It was his first day of school, and the Jewish communities of medieval Europe had decided that a child's first meeting with the Word of God deserved to be remembered with the whole body.

A prayer book compiled by a student of the great scholar Rashi, known today as the Mahzor Vitry, describes what happened next. The teacher set the boy on his lap and showed him a small slate on which the Hebrew alphabet had been written, along with a few short verses of Scripture. He read the letters aloud one at a time, and the child repeated each one after him. Then the teacher spread honey over the letters, and the boy licked the slate clean. Afterward he was given little cakes kneaded with honey and an egg with verses written on its shell, and he ate those too. Historians who have studied the ceremony, such as Ivan Marcus of Yale University, point out how deliberate it all was. Parents and teachers wanted the very first taste of God's Word in a child's life to be sweet, so that the memory would stay in his mouth long after the lesson ended.

Somewhere behind that sticky slate stands today's reading. Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, 176 verses arranged as an alphabetical poem. It has twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every one of the eight lines in a stanza begins with the same letter. In a sense, the whole psalm is itself an alphabet slate, a child's primer of devotion from the first letter to the last. Our stanza belongs to mem, the thirteenth letter, and it sits near the very center of the poem.

The writer never gives his name, but he tells us a good deal about his life. Earlier in the psalm he says that rulers sit together and slander him (Psalm 119:23), that arrogant people mock him without restraint (Psalm 119:51), and that he has been laid low in the dust (Psalm 119:25). This is a man under real pressure, with enemies who know his name. And yet when he reaches the middle of his alphabet, he breaks into something close to a love song: "Oh, how I love your law! I meditate on it all day long" (Psalm 119:97). A few lines later he reaches for the image those medieval teachers would one day put on a slate.

"How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" (Psalm 119:103)

The word the psalmist uses for "meditate" in verse 97 is worth a closer look. In Hebrew it is siach, and it describes the mind turning something over and over, often aloud, often without being able to stop. The same word appears in places you might not expect. When Hannah prays so intensely at the tabernacle that the priest Eli assumes she is drunk, she explains, "I have been praying here out of my great anguish and grief" (1 Samuel 1:16), and the word behind "anguish" is a form of siach. When David hides in a cave from those hunting him, he writes, "I pour out before him my complaint" (Psalm 142:2), and "complaint" is that same word again.

One way to read this is that siach names a faculty every human being already has. It is the part of us that rehearses a worry at two in the morning, replays a hurtful conversation while we wash the dishes, and calculates the unpaid bills again on the long ride home. Hannah used it for her sorrow and David used it for his trouble. The writer of Psalm 119, a man with his own share of enemies and dust, took that same restless habit of mind and gave it a better place to return to. Everyone meditates on something all day long; the psalmist taught his restless mind to come home to the words of God.

That is also where the honey comes in. The little boy on his teacher's lap did not love the Hebrew alphabet when he woke up that morning. The letters were strange shapes to him, and the sweetness was given to teach him something he could not yet feel on his own. Our own bodies work in a similar way. Researchers who study children's eating habits have found that a young child often needs to taste an unfamiliar food many times, sometimes ten or more, before it stops seeming strange and starts seeming good. Taste is partly a gift and partly something learned through patient, repeated contact.

Psalm 119 seems to know this. The sweetness of verse 103 does not appear in the first line of the stanza. It comes after the psalmist has spent several lines describing a long, steady life with God's words: keeping them with him (verse 98), obeying them (verse 100), keeping his feet from evil paths (verse 101), and refusing to wander from them (verse 102). Then, just before he speaks of honey, he says something tender: "I have not departed from your laws, for you yourself have taught me" (Psalm 119:102). The Hebrew is emphatic, with the sense of "you, you yourself." The psalmist pictures God as the teacher who sets him on his lap, points to each letter, and waits while he repeats it. The sweetness he now tastes was patiently given by the One who taught him.

The rest of Scripture carries the same flavor. Psalm 19 says of God's decrees that "they are sweeter than honey, than honey from the honeycomb" (Psalm 19:10). When the prophet Ezekiel is called to speak to a stubborn people, God hands him a scroll and tells him to eat it, and Ezekiel reports, "So I ate it, and it tasted as sweet as honey in my mouth" (Ezekiel 3:3). The Bible consistently describes God's words as food to be taken in slowly and savored, which is why verse 99 can make its bold claim that meditation gives the psalmist "more insight than all my teachers." Understanding grows in the one who lingers.

Many of us come to the Bible the way a tired person eats at a fast-food counter, standing up, looking at the clock, and hardly tasting anything. Others of us have known seasons when the words felt dry as chalk, and we quietly wondered whether something was wrong with us. If that describes you, the medieval slate offers real comfort. The sweetness is learned, and God himself is the patient teacher. You are still on his lap, and he is still pointing at the letters.

A gentle way to begin is to choose one verse in the morning and carry it with you through the day, perhaps verse 103 itself. Write it on a scrap of paper in your wallet or set it as the lock screen on your phone. Then, when your mind begins its familiar siach, circling the deadline, the remittance that has not arrived, or the child who has not called, turn that same restless attention back to the verse. Let it dissolve slowly, the way a piece of sampalok candy lasts longest when you stop chewing and let it melt on your tongue. You may need to return to it ten times before lunch, and that is perfectly fine, since that is how a taste is learned.

Nine centuries ago, a small boy went home from his first day of school with honey on his lips and the alphabet in his head. Tonight, before you sleep, you can do something very much like it. Read verse 103 once more, slowly, and thank the One who taught you to read it. He has been setting honey on the page for a very long time, and he delights to watch his children discover how sweet his words can be.

articles.title: The Relative No One Counted On
articles.dek: An old proverb warns against moving a widow's boundary stone. The reason it gives turns out to be one of the most tender words in the Hebrew Bible.
articles.quote: The fatherless are never as unprotected as they look, because God has made himself their next of kin.
articles.body:
In 1996, a geneticist named Diana Bianchi and her colleagues found something in women's blood that seemed out of place. They detected male cells, carrying a Y chromosome, in mothers who had given birth to sons. Some of those sons were grown men by then, and in one woman the cells were still circulating twenty-seven years after her boy was born. During pregnancy, it turns out, a small number of the baby's cells cross the placenta into the mother's body, and some of them stay for decades. Scientists call this fetal microchimerism, after the chimera of Greek myth, a creature made of more than one animal.

A later discovery was even more surprising. In 2012, cardiologist Hina Chaudhry and her team at Mount Sinai in New York studied pregnant mice whose unborn pups carried a glowing green marker. When the mothers suffered heart damage, the researchers examined the injured hearts and found green cells gathered at the wound. The child's cells had traveled to the place where the mother was hurt, and some of them had become new heart tissue, beating along with hers. Researchers are still working out what this means for human mothers, but the picture is a lovely one. Hidden in her own body, a mother carries a relative who comes running when she is wounded.

I thought of those small green cells while reading a short saying in Proverbs 23. It belongs to a section that begins at Proverbs 22:17, which the NIV titles "Thirty Sayings of the Wise." These read like a father's warnings to a son about to go out into the world. Many scholars have pointed out that several of them resemble an older Egyptian teaching called the Instruction of Amenemope, which also warns against shifting a neighbor's boundary marker. Israel's wise men seem to have taken a moral truth their whole region recognized and set it on firmer ground by attaching the name and character of the LORD to it.

The verses just before are full of practical street sense. Proverbs 23:6–8 warns about dining with "a begrudging host," the kind of man who says "Eat and drink" while privately counting the cost of every bite, so that "his heart is not with you" (Proverbs 23:7). Verse 9 adds that it is useless to pour good advice into a fool who will only scorn it. Then, in verses 10 and 11, the father's voice grows more serious. He turns from table manners to a crime that, in ancient Israel, could take away a family's whole future.

Picture a small farming village in the hill country of Judah. There were no satellite maps and no land registry office down the road. A family's fields were marked by stones set in the earth, often by a great-grandfather, and the whole village knew where those lines ran. The land was more than property. Each family's plot was understood as its share of the inheritance God had given Israel, which is why the law said, "Do not move your neighbor's boundary stone set up by your predecessors in the inheritance you receive" (Deuteronomy 19:14). Now picture a widow whose husband has died and whose sons are still small. Her neighbor's plow goes out before dawn, and over a few seasons the stone between their fields drifts a meter, then two. She has no husband to walk the line and argue at the town gate, and her neighbor is counting on exactly that.

"Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless, for their Defender is strong; he will take up their case against you." (Proverbs 23:10–11)

The word translated "Defender" is the Hebrew go'el, and it carries the warmth of family. A go'el was a kinsman-redeemer, the nearest male relative whose duty was to rescue a family member in trouble. If a relative fell into poverty and had to sell land, "their nearest relative is to come and redeem what they have sold" (Leviticus 25:25). The most famous go'el in Scripture is Boaz, who bought back the field of Naomi's late husband and married Ruth, the young widow. When their son was born, the women of Bethlehem said to Naomi, "Praise be to the LORD, who this day has not left you without a guardian-redeemer" (Ruth 4:14).

That background makes this proverb quietly astonishing. The fatherless were, by definition, the people who had lost their go'el. The man moving the stone assumed that no relative would ever stand up for them. The proverb answers that the LORD himself has stepped into that empty place in the family line. He is their kinsman, and he is "strong," from a Hebrew root used for firmness and might. The phrase "take up their case" comes from the language of the courtroom, where it describes pleading a lawsuit, so the picture is of God as the orphan's relative and lawyer at once. Job reached for the same word in his darkest hour: "I know that my redeemer lives, and that in the end he will stand on the earth" (Job 19:25).

The gospel carries this truth further than the old sages could have imagined. A go'el had to be kin, a blood relative, and so God became our kin. "Since the children have flesh and blood, he too shared in their humanity" (Hebrews 2:14), and so "Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters" (Hebrews 2:11). Paul writes that God sent his Son "born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under law, that we might receive adoption to sonship" (Galatians 4:4–5). Like those cells that cross into the mother and stay, the Son of God took on our flesh and has never laid it aside. The risen Christ still bears our humanity, and Scripture says that when we fail, "we have an advocate with the Father" (1 John 2:1). He goes to the place of the wound because he belongs to the family.

Filipinos know the boundary stone problem well. A lolo dies, the land title was never transferred, and years later a cousin has fenced off a few extra meters. A widowed tita is pressed to sign papers she does not understand. Sometimes the moved stone is not land at all. It is the kasambahay whose salary is paid late because she would never dare complain, or the small loan from a widow that gets quietly forgotten. This proverb asks each of us to check our own fences. The people with no one to speak for them have Someone, and he is watching the line.

It also invites us to share in his work. The God who is a go'el to the fatherless often does his defending through his people. This week you might help a widow in your parish sort out her documents at the Registry of Deeds, or pay the helper on the day you promised, or simply ask a child whose father is gone how school is going and then actually listen. These are small acts, but they make the family of God visible to someone who has felt alone in the world.

And if you are the one whose stones have been moved, whose share was taken, whose case no one would argue, this proverb was written for you as well. The fatherless are never as unprotected as they look, because God has made himself their next of kin. Your Defender is strong, he knows exactly where your boundary was meant to run, and he has already taken up your case. You can rest tonight knowing that a Relative is on his way to the place where you are hurt.
